item.title: Childhood Cancer Risk After Assisted Reproductive Technology
item.description: This extended follow-up of a cohort study reassesses associations between use of assisted reproductive technology (ART) and childhood cancer overall and by ART modality and cancer type.

item.title: The US Opioid Overdose Epidemic at a Crossroad
item.description: Reducing the opioid supply has been an important pillar of US public health overdose prevention efforts. Initiatives focused on reducing opioid prescribing, such as prescription drug monitoring programs and pain management guideline changes, have been implemented concurrently with observed declines in opioid prescribing since 2010. More recent declines in opioid-related deaths (driven largely by declines in fentanyl deaths) to prepandemic rates have prompted further examination for potential explanations of success and opportunities to better address the opioid overdose epidemic.

item.title: Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Steatotic Liver Disease in Children and Adolescents
item.description: This JAMA Insights discusses the diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease in children and adolescents.

item.title: National and County-Level Trends in Opioid Dispensing
item.description: This cross-sectional study uses US pharmacy data to examine national and county-level opioid dispensing patterns from 2019 through 2025.

item.title: Nonfatal Drug Overdoses and Naloxone Use
item.description: This study uses national emergency medical service (EMS) data to examine temporal changes in nonfatal overdoses and naloxone administrations by EMS clinicians and laypersons relative to the US national peak in overdose deaths.

item.title: Prone Positioning for Infants With Bronchiolitis and HFNC Support
item.description: To the Editor The PROPOSITIS trial was a large study evaluating prone positioning in infants with bronchiolitis receiving high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) support. Although the primary outcome was not statistically significant, the observed effect size suggests that further investigation remains warranted.

item.title: Prone Positioning for Infants With Bronchiolitis and HFNC Support—Reply
item.description: In Reply We thank Drs van Egmond and Mulier for their letter about the PROPOSITIS study. They raise an important point regarding the need to report the prone positioning procedure and the effects of prone positioning beyond transpulmonary pressure gradients.

item.title: Patient Information: Childhood Obesity
item.description: This JAMA Patient Page describes how childhood obesity is defined, how common it is, and the risk factors and health conditions associated with childhood obesity.

item.title: Social History
item.description: Your emergence was always in light blue cotton nightclothes, shuffling already stooped to pick up the paper. You did your primary survey right side, above the fold but no news was good enough; you salvaged the Travel section and threw the rest away, and so it was since your wife died or your hair greyed— I knew no more of your story than this morning ritual, than that you wasted money on a newspaper subscription when you should have bought a Lonely Planet guide.

item.title: “He Lives Alone”: The Social History and Detachment in Poetry and Medicine
item.description: The poem “Social History” considers how we distance ourselves from others. Although critiques of medical care frequently bemoan unfeeling clinical detachment, here distancing begins outside of the hospital in the very act of observing and then in the writing of the poem itself. The speaker blithely describes a man through the morning ritual she watches: he emerges from his home in “light/blue cotton nightclothes,” retrieves the newspaper, saves the Travel section, discards the rest. This knowledge is intimate yet incomplete, neighborly yet espied, even slightly invasive. The poem, then, implicates itself as almost a failed “social history,” describing a life observed but not understood. This disconnect is then mirrored in the emergency room, where clinical language only augments distancing. “Elderly male, single GSW to the right forehead,/likely self-inflicted./Allergies, past medical,/past surgical, medications:/all unknown,” the speaker, now in medical garb, rattles off, accurately and efficiently. Yet poetry manages to redeem here, not just by illuminating, but attempting to undo that separation, in the juxtaposition of the deceased’s blue nightclothes with the speaker’s blue scrubs; while “right side, above the fold,” where we imagine him reading about far-off lands never visited with his deceased wife, becomes “right temple, above bloodied eye creases,” locus of the mortal self-injury that reunites them. Poetry abets insouciant bystander becoming conflicted physician, the casual observation becoming a wound—and so the neighbor whose story was always visible but never fully read, having become another nameless suicide, is ironically, and poignantly, finally seen.

item.title: Obesity in Children Aged 2 to 12 Years
item.description: This narrative review examines obesity in children aged 2 to 12 years, including its epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, and treatment, such as intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment and approved pharmacotherapies.

item.title: Reassessing Lumbar Punctures for Very Young Febrile Infants
item.description: This Viewpoint examines the use of lumbar puncture in febrile young infants and how recent evidence and tools, such as novel blood biomarkers, have shaped understanding of the procedure.

item.title: Incorrect Affiliation
item.description: In the Research Letter titled “Characteristics of Patients Choosing Intravenous Moderate Sedation for IUD Placement,” published online September 17, 2026, the affiliation for Tanvi Mehta should have been The University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Minneapolis. This article was corrected online.

item.title: Individualized Cardiac Index–Guided Hemodynamic Therapy in High-Risk Patients
item.description: This multicenter, single-blind, superiority randomized clinical trial compares the effects of individualized cardiac index–guided hemodynamic therapy vs routine hemodynamic therapy on outcomes in high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery.

item.title: Individualized Cardiac Index–Guided Hemodynamic Therapy in High-Risk Patients Undergoing Elective Major Abdominal Surgery Research Summary
item.description: This trial evaluated whether individualized cardiac index–guided hemodynamic therapy improved outcomes in high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery.

item.title: Therapy for Adults With Complicated Urinary Tract Infection
item.description: This Clinical Guidelines Synopsis summarizes the 2025 Infectious Diseases Society of America guidelines on treatment and management of complicated urinary tract infections in adults.

item.title: Accessibility of Publicly Posted Kidney Transplant Waitlist Criteria Under IOTA
item.description: This study evaluated baseline transparency compliance among transplant centers participating in the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ (CMS) Increasing Organ Transplant Access (IOTA) model to assess the presence and functional accessibility of their publicly posted selection criteria.

item.title: Illicit Injectable Peptides
item.description: To the Editor Dr Piatkowski and colleagues describe how unapproved injectable peptides are promoted for muscle growth, recovery, and antiaging, despite limited human evidence. The same phenomenon is already emerging in Brazil, demonstrating how rapidly digital markets can carry unsupported health claims across national borders.

item.title: Illicit Injectable Peptides—Reply
item.description: In Reply We thank Dr Janovsky for highlighting the emergence of illicit peptide markets in Brazil and for extending the discussion beyond the jurisdictions considered in our original Viewpoint. Janovsky’s observations reinforce our central argument that the rapid expansion of unapproved peptide use is no longer a country-specific regulatory issue, but an increasingly global public health challenge. The Brazilian experience is striking because it mirrors patterns emerging elsewhere. Illicit peptides are increasingly marketed online using remarkably consistent narratives centered on recovery, muscle growth, healthy aging, and health optimization, despite limited human evidence supporting these claims. As Janovsky notes, concerns extend beyond efficacy to product quality, manufacturing standards, and unsupported therapeutic claims.

item.title: CD36 Variant and the Genetic Landscape of Dilated Cardiomyopathy
item.description: This multicohort genetic association study compares the contribution of a CD36 nonsense variant to risk of dilated cardiomyopathy vs the contribution of truncating variants in TTN and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other established genes for dilated cardiomyopathy.

item.title: Testing for Alzheimer Disease in Asymptomatic Adults
item.description: This Viewpoint discusses the uncertain prognostic value of testing for Alzheimer disease biomarkers in asymptomatic individuals and warns of the possible insurance, employment, financial, and psychological repercussions of positive results of such tests.
